policy_title: Make it Easier to Switch to Electric Vehicles
stated: Make it cheaper and easier for drivers to switch to electric vehicles by rapidly rolling out far more charging points (including residential on-street points and ultra-fast chargers at service stations), supporting new charging points with an upgraded National Grid, reintroducing the plug-in car grant, cutting VAT on public charging to 5%, and restoring the requirement that every new car and small van sold from 2030 is zero-emission.

source.quote: Make it cheaper and easier for drivers to switch to electric vehicles by rapidly rolling out far more charging points, reintroducing the plug-in car grant, and restoring the requirement that every new car and small van sold from 2030 is zero-emission. Make it easy and cheap to charge electric vehicles by: Rolling out far more charging points, including residential on-street points and ultra-fast chargers at service stations. Supporting new charging points with an upgraded National Grid and a stepchange in local grid capacity. Cutting VAT on public charging to 5%.

bearing_set.reason: The 2030 ZEV mandate restoration, infrastructure rollout, and financial incentives are all designed to accelerate fleet electrification, directly affecting emissions trajectory and urban air quality (NOx, particulates).

Cutting VAT on public charging from 20% to 5% and reintroducing the plug-in car grant are explicit price interventions that reduce running and purchase costs for households switching to EVs, with a real effect on disposable income and the inflation basket.

The plug-in car grant (previously costing hundreds of millions annually) and the VAT revenue foregone on public charging are material fiscal costs; the grid upgrade represents a large capital commitment — both affect the funded/borrowed balance.

The ZEV mandate provides regulatory certainty for UK automotive and supply-chain investment; the grid upgrade is productive infrastructure; and reduced reliance on imported oil improves long-run living standards — real dual-horizon prosperity effects.

Grants and VAT reliefs on new EVs (still premium-priced assets) disproportionately benefit higher-income households who can afford new vehicles, creating a plausible regressive distributional effect on the rich-poor gap.

membership_note: Five fundamentals bear genuinely: the environmental core (O6), household cost effect (O2), fiscal cost (O12), long-run prosperity signal (O13), and distributional skew of the subsidy instruments (O14). O10 was considered (ZEV mandate constrains new-car sales) but the constraint falls on manufacturers/dealers rather than individual liberty directly, so it does not clear the non-negligible personal-liberty bar. O11 was considered but the VAT cut reduces prices rather than take-home pay and is properly housed in O2.
